more_info.overview: Curcumin is the principal yellow pigment in turmeric. Food-grade E100 is a concentrated extract containing curcumin and related pigments. It adds yellow to orange colour to foods. The specified material is supplied as yellow powder or crystalline material.
more_info.origin: Plant-derived. Ground turmeric rhizomes are extracted with solvents, and the extract is crystallised to concentrate the colouring compounds.
more_info.daily_intake: 0–3 mg/kg body weight per day (JECFA, 2003); 3 mg/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2010).
more_info.side_effects:
At food-use exposures, EFSA retained its ADI; its 2014 assessment nevertheless estimated that some high-consuming toddlers and children could reach or exceed it. These are exposure estimates, not observed symptoms.
At high experimental doses, reduced weight gain in second-generation rats was the endpoint used to set the ADI. This animal evidence does not establish the same effect at ordinary human food intakes.
more_info.uses:
Examples in the EU food-use list include certain other confectionery including breath freshening microsweets; chewing gum; decorations, coatings and fillings, except fruit-based fillings covered by category 4.2.4; flavoured drinks; flavoured fermented milk products including heat-treated products; unripened cheese excluding products falling in category 16.
The entries apply to particular food categories and may limit the amount, the preparation or the way it is used; they do not show how often the additive appears in retail products.
more_info.dietary_restrictions: The pigment is extracted from turmeric, a plant, so the pigment itself is compatible with vegan and vegetarian diets.

more_info.overview: Turmeric colour is the ground rhizome of Curcuma longa, the same plant material used as a spice. It contains a mixture of plant constituents rather than only the isolated curcumin pigment. FDA defines this preparation separately from turmeric oleoresin and allows its use to colour foods under manufacturing and food-standard conditions. Its food role can therefore involve both the colour and the flavour of the ground spice.
more_info.origin: Plant-derived. The colour material described by FDA is made by grinding turmeric rhizomes.
more_info.daily_intake: No ADI allocated for turmeric (JECFA, 1986). JECFA noted that turmeric is often treated as a food rather than a food additive.
more_info.uses: Used as a spice in foods such as curries and mustard. FDA permits turmeric as a colour in foods generally, subject to standards of identity and good manufacturing practice.
more_info.dietary_restrictions: Ground turmeric is a plant ingredient and is compatible with vegan and vegetarian diets.

more_info.overview: Tartrazine is a manufactured azo dye that gives food a yellow colour. It is sold in the US as FD&C Yellow No. 5. Food-grade material is a purified salt mixture meeting colour specifications. The specified material is supplied as powder or granules.
more_info.origin: Synthetic. An aromatic sulfonic acid is diazotised, coupled to a pyrazole compound, and the dye is purified as its sodium salt.
more_info.daily_intake: 0–10 mg/kg body weight per day (JECFA, 2016). EFSA retained 7.5 mg/kg body weight per day in 2009; these are distinct assessments.
more_info.side_effects:
At food-use levels, EFSA reported intolerance reactions in a small fraction of people; reactions can occur within the ADI. Studies of colour mixtures with sodium benzoate do not establish that tartrazine alone causes behavioural changes.
At high experimental doses, reduced body weight in rats was the endpoint for JECFA's 2016 ADI. This animal evidence does not establish the same effect at food-use levels in humans.
more_info.uses:

more_info.overview: Quinoline Yellow WS is a yellow food dye based on sulfonated quinophthalone compounds. It is a mixture of colouring salts rather than a single pure molecule. Its role in food is to supply yellow colour. The specified material is supplied as yellow powder or granules.

High-dose animal toxicity studies supplied the basis for the ADIs. They do not demonstrate comparable effects at normal human food intakes.

more_info.overview: Cochineal extract and carmine are red colours whose main pigment is carminic acid. Carmine is a metal complex made from that pigment. In foods these materials produce red shades. The specified material is supplied as deep red powder or liquid.
more_info.origin: Animal-derived, specifically from dried female cochineal insects. Extraction releases carminic acid; reaction with aluminium forms carmine, sometimes with other metal ions.
more_info.daily_intake: 2.5 mg carminic acid/kg body weight per day (EFSA, 2015). This expresses the earlier 5 mg carmine/kg body weight ADI in terms of carminic acid content.
more_info.side_effects:
At food-use levels, allergic reactions to cochineal/carmine can occur; EFSA could not establish a threshold dose for allergy. Residual proteins were identified as a reason to improve purification.
The animal toxicity studies reviewed by EFSA did not justify lowering the existing ADI; this does not remove the separate allergy risk.
more_info.uses:

more_info.dietary_restrictions: Not suitable for vegan or vegetarian diets because the colour is extracted from insects.
more_info.precautions: EFSA identified allergenic material in E120 and recommended manufacturing purification steps because no allergy threshold could be established.

more_info.overview: Citrus Red No. 2 is a synthetic azo dye whose principal component is a dimethoxyphenylazo naphthol compound. Its US food application is unusually narrow: colouring the skin of mature oranges not intended for processing, with the stated packinghouse exception. The limit is 2 mg/kg calculated from the weight of the whole fruit. It is not a general-purpose colour for drinks, sweets or other citrus products under that regulation.
more_info.daily_intake: No safe intake determined; JECFA concluded that this colour should not be used as a food additive (1969).
more_info.side_effects:
Human effects at the restricted food-use level were not established in the reviewed JECFA monograph.
Animal studies reviewed in 1969 reported bladder changes and other toxicity at experimental doses, with inconsistent tumour findings. JECFA considered the unexplained results sufficient to reject food-additive use; this is not proof of cancer at the permitted orange-skin exposure.
more_info.uses: US authorization covers the skins of mature oranges not intended for processing, with a limit of 2 mg/kg calculated on the whole fruit.

EU permissions include processed cheese, fruit and vegetable preparations excluding compote, processed fish and fishery products including molluscs and crustaceans.
more_info.uses:
Examples in the EU food-use list include certain other confectionery including breath freshening microsweets; chewing gum; decorations, coatings and fillings, except fruit-based fillings covered by category 4.2.4; flavoured drinks; flavoured fermented milk products including heat-treated products; unripened cheese excluding products falling in category 16.
The entries apply to particular food categories and may limit the amount, the preparation or the way it is used; they do not show how often the additive appears in retail products.
more_info.side_effects:
In 2026, JECFA noted that a high dietary exposure estimate for toddlers exceeded its existing intake limit.
The limit was based on animal evidence; exceedance alone does not establish a clinical effect.

more_info.overview: Titanium dioxide is an inorganic oxide used to give foods a white colour; food-grade material differs from the raw mineral ore used in manufacture. Food-grade preparations may have small surface coatings of alumina or silica. The specified material is supplied as white powder. The specification describes it as effectively insoluble in water.
more_info.daily_intake: ADI classified as not limited or not specified (JECFA, 2023). EFSA could not establish food-use safety in 2021.
more_info.origin: An inorganic titanium oxide pigment made by sulphate or chloride processing. Food-grade preparations may have small surface coatings of alumina or silica.
more_info.side_effects:
The bodies reached different food-use conclusions: EFSA could not rule out DNA damage in 2021, while FDA reports that JECFA's 2023 evaluation found food use safe.
FDA did not identify a genotoxicity concern and noted no cancer effect in the cited long-term animal studies; these findings do not remove the EU uncertainty.
more_info.uses: FDA-authorised uses include bakery products and confectionery, subject to the US limit of 1% of food weight.

The principal material is a galactomannan polysaccharide. The specified material is supplied as white powder. The specification identifies water solubility as one of its properties.

more_info.dietary_restrictions: The specified starting material is plant derived and compatible with vegetarian and vegan diets. The specification does not establish halal or kosher certification.
more_info.side_effects:
EFSA found no concern for assessed food uses.
Animal studies found no adverse effects at the highest tested doses.

more_info.overview: Gum ghatti is a tree-exudate gum also called Indian gum. It comes from wounds in the bark of Anogeissus latifolia and forms viscous preparations in water. Its food role includes emulsifying ingredients so that dispersed components remain mixed. FDA specifies use in non-alcoholic beverages and beverage bases, with a different maximum for other food categories. The source tree and gum identity distinguish it from gum arabic and other plant gums.
more_info.origin: Plant-derived exudate collected from wounds in the bark of Anogeissus latifolia, a tree found in India and Sri Lanka.
more_info.uses: An emulsifier in non-alcoholic beverages and beverage bases, with a US maximum of 0.2% in the served food. The FDA regulation sets a 0.1% maximum for other food categories.
more_info.dietary_restrictions: The gum itself is plant derived and compatible with vegan and vegetarian diets. This origin does not establish halal or kosher certification of a commercial preparation.

more_info.overview: Peptones are mixtures of amino acids and short protein chains obtained by partial breakdown of proteins. The starting proteins may come from animal tissues, milk, eggs or soy. more_info.overview: Gelatine is a mixture of animal-derived proteins obtained by partially breaking down collagen. It absorbs water and softens in cold water, then dissolves when heated. On cooling, the solution forms a gel, which explains its gelling function in food. JECFA also identifies stabilising, emulsifying and crystallisation-control functions. The commercial ingredient can be supplied as sheets, flakes or powder, with grades that differ in gel strength.
more_info.origin: Gelatine is manufactured by partially hydrolysing collagen from animal tissues such as skin, tendons, ligaments and bones. The protein is extracted and processed into dried sheets, flakes or powder. It is an animal-derived ingredient; the specification does not identify a single animal species for every product.
more_info.dietary_restrictions: Ordinary gelatine is made from animal collagen and is therefore unsuitable for vegan and vegetarian diets. Halal and kosher suitability depend on the animal species, slaughter and processing arrangements, and product certification; the E code alone does not establish those conditions.

more_info.overview: 4-Hexylresorcinol is an organic resorcinol derivative used to control browning in crustaceans. more_info.daily_intake: No ADI established because the available database was insufficient (EFSA, 2014). EFSA accepted the limited crustacean application with residues not exceeding 2 mg/kg in crustacean meat; this residue limit is not a daily intake limit.
more_info.side_effects:
At the assessed food exposure: EFSA considered the margin between estimated dietary exposure and the experimental toxicity benchmark sufficient for the limited shrimp and crustacean application in 2014. This was a regulatory assessment, not evidence from a trial showing that every exposure has no effects.
At higher experimental exposure: mouse studies identified kidney damage as the most sensitive toxicity endpoint. EFSA found the data inadequate for an ADI and required additional reproductive-toxicity data before any expansion of use.

Their technological action is protein breakdown, with the resulting effect depending on the food process and enzyme preparation. An evaluation of one source or enzyme cannot describe every member of the family.
